PRODUCT BACKLOG / CONSULTING PORTFOLIO

A clear direction.
A plan to build it.

My Agile plan for evolving this website into a credible, early-career AI consulting portfolio—connecting my Information Systems background, customer-facing experience, and technical projects.

Explore the backlog ↓

Proposed plan · November 17, 2026 · 3 themes / 6 epics / 12 user stories

01 / PRODUCT GOAL

Help people understand
what I can contribute.

Product vision: A professor, recruiter, or prospective project partner can understand my direction, inspect evidence of my work, and find a clear next step.

Audience: Technical reviewers need code and contribution details. Project partners need clear problems, scope, and deliverables. Professors need traceable research and honest reflection.

Starting point

The current site already has career research, a project directory, and an educational Agile example. This backlog proposes refinements and a consulting-focused structure; it does not mark that work as complete.

Scope: A public-facing portfolio experience is the design goal. The hosted site is currently public. Its portfolio claims and source links should be reviewed with that audience in mind.

PLANNING CONVENTION

Theme → screen-based epic → meaningful user action → implementation tasks. As in my Agile example, epics group screens for illustration. Real teams can use capability-based epics across multiple pages. The proposed pages below can also begin as sections before becoming separate routes.

Read the Google and Accenture employer personas informing this plan →

02 / THEMES

Three outcomes
guide the work.

T1

Make my direction clear

Position an aspiring AI consultant around useful problems and a transparent approach.

T2

Build trust through evidence

Let projects, sources, and honest reflection demonstrate my current capabilities.

T3

Make collaboration easy

Give visitors a clear next step and learn from their feedback.

03 / PRIORITIZED BACKLOG

From visitor needs
to reviewable tasks.

All stories below are proposed. “Must” defines the first useful portfolio release; “Should” adds depth in the next iteration. Tasks do not have completion checkboxes because delivery needs evidence and review.

12 stories across 6 epics

T1 → E1 / PROPOSED SCREEN

Home / positioning

Help a visitor understand my focus and choose a useful next step.

S1.1 Understand my focus / Must · Proposed

As a prospective collaborator, I want to understand my AI and Information Systems focus so I can decide whether to explore my work.

Target: Iteration 1 · Depends on: None

Acceptance criteria

The hero identifies Ximena, Information Systems at NJIT, expected graduation January 2029, and an aspiring AI consulting / FDE direction. It makes no claim of established client experience.

Tasks

  1. S1.1.T1 — Draft a concise positioning statement.
  2. S1.1.T2 — Connect the hero to Projects and Consulting Approach.
  3. S1.1.T3 — Check education details and remove unsupported claims.
S1.2 Choose my next step / Must · Proposed

As a first-time visitor, I want to find the main areas of the portfolio so I can reach relevant evidence quickly.

Target: Iteration 1 · Depends on: S1.1

Acceptance criteria

Career research, projects, consulting approach, and contact are reachable through clearly labeled links. Links work on narrow screens and by keyboard.

Tasks

  1. S1.2.T1 — Simplify the main navigation.
  2. S1.2.T2 — Add descriptive calls to action.
  3. S1.2.T3 — Check page destinations and keyboard focus.

T1 → E2 / PROPOSED SCREEN

Consulting approach

Explain the kinds of problems I want to help solve and how I would work.

S2.1 Explore proposed capabilities / Must · Proposed

As a prospective collaborator, I want to see the types of work I am developing toward so I can assess whether a conversation would be useful.

Target: Iteration 1 · Depends on: S1.1

Acceptance criteria

The page describes workflow discovery, scoped AI prototyping, and evaluation/documentation as developing capabilities. Each has an example deliverable and a clear scope limit.

Tasks

  1. S2.1.T1 — Draft three capability descriptions.
  2. S2.1.T2 — Connect each to relevant existing work or a labeled future project.
  3. S2.1.T3 — Review wording so learning goals are distinct from delivered services.
S2.2 Understand the process / Should · Proposed

As a project partner, I want to understand the steps from discovery to handoff so I know how the work could be scoped and reviewed.

Persona links: P2

Target: Iteration 2 · Depends on: S2.1

Acceptance criteria

Discover → Define → Prototype → Evaluate → Handoff is explained. Each step names an output and a feedback checkpoint; no guaranteed business results are promised.

Tasks

  1. S2.2.T1 — Write an example discovery brief and success criteria.
  2. S2.2.T2 — Show the five process steps with deliverables.
  3. S2.2.T3 — Add a change-request and scope-review checkpoint.

T2 → E3 / PROPOSED SCREEN

Project directory

Let reviewers find relevant evidence without treating every exercise as a finished product.

S3.1 Browse relevant projects / Must · Proposed

As a technical reviewer, I want to filter projects by skill and project type so I can find evidence relevant to a role or problem.

Persona links: P1

Target: Iteration 1 · Depends on: None

Acceptance criteria

Project cards show a short summary, relevant skills, repository link, and an honest status. Filters distinguish software, web/design, research, and introductory exercises; clearing filters restores all projects.

Tasks

  1. S3.1.T1 — Reuse the reviewed public-repository summaries.
  2. S3.1.T2 — Add category metadata and accessible filter controls.
  3. S3.1.T3 — Check combined filters, reset, and an empty-result state.
S3.2 Inspect source evidence / Must · Proposed

As a technical reviewer, I want to open the source behind a project claim so I can assess the evidence myself.

Persona links: P1

Target: Iteration 1 · Depends on: S3.1

Acceptance criteria

Repository and evidence links are labeled and match each summary. Team projects identify shared ownership. Private repositories and empty exercises are not presented as completed client work.

Tasks

  1. S3.2.T1 — Verify the source link for each featured claim.
  2. S3.2.T2 — Keep starter, unfinished, and team labels visible.
  3. S3.2.T3 — Check external links and document the review date.

T2 → E4 / PROPOSED SCREEN

Project case study

Explain a problem, the work, and the evidence behind it.

S4.1 Understand a case study / Must · Proposed

As a portfolio reviewer, I want to understand a project’s problem, approach, and result so I can assess relevant engineering and delivery reasoning.

Persona links: P1, P2

Target: Iteration 2 · Depends on: S3.2

Acceptance criteria

At least one case study contains context, problem, scope, approach, evidence, and limitations. Results distinguish observed behavior from proposed benefits; no client, metric, or outcome is invented. Technical reviewers can find the implementation flow, source links, and a documented check or an explicit evidence gap. Delivery reviewers can find intended users, scope, and the evidence or unmeasured status of the outcome.

Tasks

  1. S4.1.T1 — Choose one repository with sufficient evidence.
  2. S4.1.T2 — Write the problem, implementation flow, and source links.
  3. S4.1.T3 — Add verification evidence, outcome labels, and a verified screenshot or demo when available.
  4. S4.1.T4 — Review the case study using both persona perspectives.
S4.2 Understand my contribution / Must · Proposed

As a hiring manager, I want to distinguish my contribution and learning from team or AI assistance so I can assess my actual experience.

Persona links: P1, P2

Target: Iteration 2 · Depends on: S4.1

Acceptance criteria

The case study labels individual, team, template, and AI-assisted work where applicable. Unconfirmed ownership is marked for confirmation; a learning reflection identifies a concrete decision or limitation.

Tasks

  1. S4.2.T1 — Ask Ximena to confirm her contribution.
  2. S4.2.T2 — Document tool or template assistance accurately.
  3. S4.2.T3 — Review every ownership and proficiency statement.

T2 → E5 / PROPOSED SCREEN

About / career direction

Connect my background and learning plan to the portfolio.

S5.1 Understand my background / Should · Proposed

As a recruiter, I want to see my education and relevant experience so I can place my projects in context.

Target: Iteration 2 · Depends on: S1.1

Acceptance criteria

Education uses the updated major and January 2029 date. Customer-facing, leadership, and programming experience is tied to the résumé without assuming old roles are current.

Tasks

  1. S5.1.T1 — Adapt the existing profile into a concise About section.
  2. S5.1.T2 — Connect transferable experience to project examples.
  3. S5.1.T3 — Confirm current role dates before changing their status.
S5.2 Review my career reasoning / Should · Proposed

As a professor or mentor, I want to follow the sources and reasoning behind my career choices so I can give specific feedback.

Target: Iteration 2 · Depends on: S5.1

Acceptance criteria

The existing three-career comparison remains linked, including source dates, eligibility limitations, and the roadmap. Proposed consulting positioning does not imply those job requirements are already met.

Tasks

  1. S5.2.T1 — Link the current career research and roadmap.
  2. S5.2.T2 — Cross-check source and timeline labels.
  3. S5.2.T3 — Ask a reviewer to locate an original employer source.

T3 → E6 / PROPOSED SCREEN

Contact / next step

Make a clear, low-friction invitation to connect.

S6.1 Start a conversation / Must · Proposed

As a prospective collaborator, I want to find a clear way to contact me so I can discuss a project, internship, or feedback.

Target: Iteration 1 · Depends on: S1.2

Acceptance criteria

A contact section links to the existing LinkedIn profile and names useful conversation topics. It does not imply that a form submission or booking system exists.

Tasks

  1. S6.1.T1 — Add the verified LinkedIn link.
  2. S6.1.T2 — Draft a short invitation and suggested message topics.
  3. S6.1.T3 — Check the link and accessible label.
S6.2 Prepare a useful inquiry / Should · Proposed

As a potential project partner, I want to see what information to include in my message so our first conversation has a clear starting point.

Persona links: P2

Target: Iteration 2 · Depends on: S6.1, S2.2

Acceptance criteria

A short checklist asks for the problem, intended users, available non-sensitive sample data, constraints, and desired outcome. It avoids requesting passwords, credentials, or private customer records.

Tasks

  1. S6.2.T1 — Write a five-item discovery checklist.
  2. S6.2.T2 — Explain that scope is agreed after discussion.
  3. S6.2.T3 — Review with one classmate for clarity.

04 / ITERATION PLAN

Release value
in small steps.

ITERATION 1 / PROPOSED MVP

Understand → inspect → connect

Goal: A visitor can understand my direction, find relevant project evidence, and reach my LinkedIn contact.

Stories: S1.1, S1.2, S2.1, S3.1, S3.2, S6.1.

Demo: Start at Home, open the consulting approach, filter Projects, inspect source evidence, and follow the contact link.

Order: Clarify positioning and project metadata first; then connect navigation and the contact path. No login or dashboard is required for this release.

ITERATION 2 / PROPOSED DEPTH

Explain → attribute → refine

Goal: A reviewer can understand a consulting process, inspect a full case study, and distinguish my contribution from assistance.

Stories: S2.2, S4.1, S4.2, S5.1, S5.2, S6.2.

Demo: Walk through one case study and its limitations, follow the career rationale, then use the discovery checklist to prepare an inquiry.

Dependency: Personal contribution details need Ximena’s confirmation before being presented as verified.

Iteration lengths and estimates are intentionally unset. Choose capacity and size stories during refinement; these groupings are proposed goals, not delivery-date commitments.

05 / DEFINITION OF DONE

Evidence before
“complete.”

For every story

  • The acceptance criteria describe working, observable behavior.
  • Project, education, and ownership claims match evidence.
  • Links, keyboard navigation, and narrow-screen layout are checked.
  • Changed interactions receive appropriate functional checks.

For each release

  • A reviewer tries the intended journey and records feedback.
  • Source changes and validation evidence are saved.
  • The deployed version matches the reviewed source.
  • Open defects and verification limits remain visible.
